svg.aria-label: Diagram: what ARC Region switch service quota parity checks do, which plans have them enabled, and what parity does and does not guarantee. AWS describes Region switch as helping you orchestrate the failover of multi-Region applications to achieve a bounded recovery time during a Regional impairment, and this release adds four capabilities: an AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block, payloads for the custom action Lambda execution block, service quota parity checks, and a wait for target group health feature for compute scaling actions, across all commercial and AWS GovCloud US Regions. The quota check addresses a failure mode the documentation states plainly: as demand grows in the active Region you might raise service quotas there to keep up but forget to request matching increases in the standby Region, and this gap can cause a healthy-looking plan to fail during execution. The central point of the post is which plans have the check turned on. Service quota checks are controlled by the serviceQuotaChecksEnabled setting on a plan, and AWS states that new plans have service quota checks enabled by default while plans created before service quota checks were available have them disabled by default. The default is therefore inverted with respect to risk, because the plans that have had the longest to accumulate quota drift are exactly the plans the check is switched off for, and a plan updated without specifying the field keeps its current setting, so ordinary maintenance will not turn it on. The second limitation is that parity is not sufficiency. AWS states that quota checks enforce parity between Regions only and do not adjust quotas based on current resource consumption. When Region switch finds a Region or account whose applied quota is lower than the matching one it can request an increase to raise the lower quota to match the higher one, so the mechanism equalises the two Regions against each other rather than against what the application actually needs. If the active Region's quota is itself too low for a full failover, which is common because an active Region's quotas are sized for its own steady state rather than for twice its traffic, then a passing parity check reports no mismatch while both Regions remain unable to take the load. The third point concerns what the feature does on the customer's behalf. The servicequotas RequestServiceQuotaIncrease and GetRequestedServiceQuotaChange permissions allow Region switch to automatically submit quota increase requests on the customer's behalf, so enabling this grants a service the ability to file requests from the account. That is bounded deliberately: to avoid exhausting the account-level limit on open quota increase requests, Region switch uses at most half of the allowed open requests, reserving the rest for the customer's own submissions, which in practice means up to 5 concurrent requests per account per Region in commercial Regions and up to 1 concurrent request per account in opt-in Regions. When the request limit is reached, additional mismatches are surfaced as warnings, and once open requests are approved or resolved Region switch submits the remaining increases on the next check cycle. Reserving half the budget for the human is thoughtful design, because a service that consumed the whole allowance would block an urgent manual request during the very event it was trying to help with. On cadence, quota checks run automatically within 30 minutes of plan creation or update and then every 24 hours, independently of plan evaluation, so a warning can appear on a plan nobody touched and between evaluations. On permissions, Region switch performs service quota checks only for plans whose execution role and any cross-account roles the plan uses include the required permissions, and this does not fail silently, because if a role is missing a required permission plan evaluation surfaces a warning identifying the missing permission instead of the quota result, which is the correct failure mode. One detail shows the feature was designed for real standby topologies: an EC2 Auto Scaling group sometimes has no running instances, such as in a standby Region scaled to zero, and in that case Region switch determines the instance families from the group's launch template or launch configuration so a parity check is still possible, while when the group has running instances Region switch uses those instances as the source of truth instead. The recommended actions are to list every Region switch plan and read its serviceQuotaChecksEnabled value rather than assuming the announcement applied to existing plans, to set it explicitly to true on older plans since an update that omits the field changes nothing, to grant the Service Quotas read permission first and decide separately about the request-submission permissions, to size the active Region's quotas against a full failover because parity against a wrong number is still parity, and to route plan evaluation warnings somewhere since the check runs on its own cadence.
svg.title: The check is on for new plans and off for the ones that have had time to drift
svg.text: A drift check, switched on for the plans that have not had time to drift.
ARC Region switch service quota parity checks — four new capabilities, one inverted default.
One sentence decides whether this release did anything for you
“New plans have service quota checks enabled by default; plans that you created before service quota
checks were available have them disabled by default.”
And it will not fix itself: “When you update a plan without specifying the field, Region switch keeps the plan's current setting.”
The failure it exists to catch
“you might raise service quotas there to keep
up, but forget to request matching increases
in your standby Region”
“a healthy-looking plan to fail during execution”
And what it does not check
“Quota checks enforce parity between Regions
only. They do not adjust quotas based on
current resource consumption.”
Parity against a number that is too low is parity.
It files the requests for you, and leaves you half the budget — which is the thoughtful part
“automatically submit quota increase requests on your behalf” — via servicequotas:RequestServiceQuotaIncrease
“uses at most half of the allowed open requests, reserving the rest for your own submissions”
commercial up to 5 concurrent / account / Region opt-in up to 1 concurrent / account
A service that spent the whole allowance would block your urgent request during the event it was helping with.
Its own clock
“within 30 minutes of plan creation or update,
and then every 24 hours”
“independent of plan evaluation” — so route it.
The right failure mode
Missing permission? “plan evaluation surfaces a
warning that identifies the missing permission”
Named warning, not a quiet pass. The opposite of #84.
This week, if you have plans older than Tuesday
List every plan, read serviceQuotaChecksEnabled, set it to true. It is a finite list and a boolean.
Then size the active Region against a full failover, because that is the number parity is copying.
A scaled-to-zero standby is read from its launch template — so pilot-light topologies, where drift is invisible, are covered.
